faq.a: Supine position increases venous return, raising left‑ventricular filling pressure and pulmonary capillary pressure, leading to fluid transudation into alveoli.
faq.q: Why does lying flat trigger PND?

faq.a: Rarely; severe COPD or high‑altitude pulmonary oedema can mimic it, but cardiac failure is the classic cause.
faq.q: Can PND occur without heart disease?

faq.a: Yes, it signals decompensated heart failure and warrants urgent diuresis and optimisation of chronic therapy.
faq.q: Is a single episode of PND enough to start treatment?

exam: What bedside findings differentiate PND from obstructive sleep apnoea? — Look for bibasal crackles, raised JVP, and relief on sitting up; sleep apnoea shows snoring and daytime somnolence.
A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with PND. What is the next immediate step? — Give a loop diuretic and position upright; arrange urgent echocardiography when possible.
How does HIV infection predispose to PND? — HIV can cause dilated cardiomyopathy and anaemia, both increasing cardiac preload and precipitating pulmonary congestion.
Why is a low‑dose ACE inhibitor preferred over high‑dose diuretics in chronic management? — ACE‑I improves remodeling and mortality; high‑dose diuretics risk electrolyte loss and renal dysfunction.
A patient with PND has a normal chest X‑ray. What does this mean? — Early pulmonary congestion may be radiographically silent; rely on clinical signs and consider ultrasound if available.
What red‑flag symptom would make you suspect an acute coronary syndrome rather than isolated PND? — New chest pressure radiating to arm/jaw with diaphoresis and ECG changes.
Explain why sitting the patient up improves PND. — Upright posture reduces venous return, lowering pulmonary capillary pressure and allowing fluid re‑absorption.

In a resource‑limited setting without BNP testing, how would you confirm heart failure as the cause of PND? — Use a combination of history (orthopnoea, PND), physical signs (crackles, JVP), and bedside ultrasound if possible.
ai.title: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnoea
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sudden breathlessness that awakens a patient from sleep, usually due to left‑sided heart failure. Recognise the pattern, identify reversible causes, and manage acutely in low‑resource settings.

b: Occurs 2–4 h after supine position
Relieved by sitting upright or using pillows
Associated with cough, frothy pink sputum in advanced cases
sections.p: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND) is an abrupt onset of severe shortness of breath that occurs several hours after lying down, often waking the patient gasping for air.

t.a: History of orthopnoea and PND episodes
t.b: Confirms cardiac origin; if absent, consider pulmonary causes

t.a: Physical exam: bibasal crackles, displaced apex beat, raised JVP
t.b: Supports left‑sided congestion; absence suggests alternative diagnosis

b: NYHA I – no limitation, PND absent
NYHA II – slight limitation, occasional PND
NYHA III – marked limitation, PND weekly
NYHA IV – symptoms at rest, daily PND
sections.p: Severity is graded by frequency and impact on daily life, using the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification.

b: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy (post‑MI)
Hypertensive heart disease
Peripartum cardiomyopathy
HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy
Severe anaemia (e.g., sickle‑cell crisis) causing high‑output failure
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the most common precipitants are conditions that raise left‑ventricular filling pressure.

b: Sudden dyspnoea waking from sleep
Cough, sometimes frothy pink sputum
Chest tightness, anxiety
Relief within minutes of sitting up
sections.p: A patient is found sitting upright, clutching the chest, with rapid, shallow breathing. The episode often follows a heavy dinner or alcohol intake.
Prioritise bedside tools; use laboratory and imaging when available.

t.b: Shows pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly; normal film does not exclude PND
Assesses B‑lines, left‑ventricular function; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs
Elevated levels support heart failure; low levels make cardiac cause less likely
Detects anaemia, infection; severe anaemia may precipitate PND

b: Persistent dyspnoea despite sitting up
Hypotension or shock
New arrhythmia or rapid atrial fibrillation
Pulmonary oedema with pink frothy sputum
Acute coronary syndrome symptoms
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention.

b: Upright positioning, supplemental oxygen (2–4 L/min via nasal cannula)
Loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) to reduce preload – avoid if severe hypovolaemia
ACE inhibitor or ARB for chronic afterload reduction – start once stable
Beta‑blocker (carvedilol) for long‑term mortality benefit – avoid in acute decompensation
Treat precipitating infection or anaemia promptly
sections.p: Treat the underlying cardiac failure first, then provide symptomatic relief.

b: Daily weight monitoring, low‑salt diet
Regular clinic review of NYHA class
Adherence to ACE‑I/ARB and diuretic regimen
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus
Screen for rheumatic fever recurrence in endemic areas
Obstructive sleep apnoea – snoring, daytime sleepiness, not relieved by sitting up
Asthma nocturnal wheeze – audible wheeze, bronchodilator response
Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia
sections.p: Distinguish PND from other nocturnal breathing problems.

b: Normal chest X‑ray early in decompensation
BNP may be low in obese patients despite heart failure
ECG may be normal in chronic mitral stenosis
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden collapse or loss of consciousness
Severe chest pain suggestive of myocardial infarction
